vignette: Dr. Linh Nguyen, a retired surgeon at the age of 77, carries with him memories that have long been a shadow over his otherwise illustrious career. Born and raised in a small village in Southeastern Asia, Dr. Nguyen immigrated to the United States for advanced medical training shortly before his 30th birthday. He has always felt a profound sense of duty to serve those in need, a value deeply rooted in the traditions of his heritage. Dr. Nguyen's PTSD stems from an incident that occurred during one of his early years at a bustling urban hospital. It was late on a Tuesday night when he had just completed a long surgery and was finally getting ready to leave for home. As he walked through the crowded emergency room, the chaos of patients screaming in pain and family members crying out for help overwhelmed him. Dr. Nguyen's attention immediately focused on a young man being brought in from a nearby shooting scene. The paramedics were desperately trying to keep him alive, but the wounds were extensive. Dr. Nguyen remembers feeling helpless as he watched the trauma team work tirelessly around him, their efforts seeming futile against the severity of the injuries. He could hear the young man's mother wailing in the background, her voice a mix of sorrow and rage. The image of her face, etched with grief and disbelief, remains vividly imprinted in his mind. In the years that followed, Dr. Nguyen continued to perform surgeries with exceptional skill, but the incident began to take its toll on him. He would often wake up in the middle of the night drenched in sweat, reliving those moments through nightmares where he sees himself unable to save anyone despite his best efforts. The sound of ambulances outside can still trigger flashbacks, leaving him feeling trapped and overwhelmed. Dr. Nguyen's wife, Mai, has noticed subtle changes in his behavior over time. He becomes easily agitated at the slightest mention of violence or trauma on the news. Even the sight of blood can send him into a state of panic. At home, he avoids crowded places, preferring to stay within the confines of their quiet neighborhood. On days when the memories are particularly vivid, Dr. Nguyen finds himself pacing back and forth in the living room late into the night. Despite his efforts to compartmentalize these experiences, they continue to seep into his professional life as well. During one of his last operations before retirement, he found it increasingly difficult to concentrate on the task at hand. Every cut and incision reminded him of that fateful day in the ER, and he felt an overwhelming urge to flee from the operating room. Dr. Nguyen's wife has become his anchor through these turbulent times. She understands the depth of his pain but sometimes feels helpless herself as she watches her husband struggle silently with his demons. Dr. Nguyen often avoids discussing what happened that night, fearing it will only bring back the anguish he tries to keep at bay. In moments of quiet reflection, Dr. Nguyen wonders if he'll ever be able to fully reconcile his past with his present. The memories still linger, a constant reminder of an event he was powerless to change. He finds solace in spending time gardening and reading books about Southeastern Asian folklore, which remind him of the resilience and strength of his cultural heritage. Though retirement has brought some peace, Dr. Nguyen knows that the trauma remains a part of who he is. The nights are still long and filled with unsettling thoughts, but there is a sense of determination to navigate this new chapter in life, one day at a time.
